did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jerusalem is called “Ariel” in this chapter and is described as “the city where David camped”—the city where David stayed.
Did you know? The description of the siege of Jerusalem uses military images of an encampment, a siege, and fortifications to illustrate the pressure that will be brought against it.

Did you know? After describing the siege and the enemies, the chapter attributes the turning point to the LORD’s intervention, portrayed through thunder, an earthquake, a whirlwind, a storm, and consuming fire.

Did you know? Jerusalem’s enemies are compared to a hungry or thirsty person who dreams of eating or drinking, but wakes up and discovers that he is still empty; this depicts the failure of those who besiege Zion.

Did you know? The image of “the sealed book” illustrates the people’s lack of understanding: one who knows how to read cannot read because the book is sealed, while one who does not know how to read is unable to read it.
Did you know? The chapter condemns outward worship that is not accompanied by heartfelt devotion, saying that the people honor the LORD with their mouths and lips, but their hearts are far from him.
Did you know? Isaiah uses the image of a potter and clay to emphasize the absurdity of people denying their Maker or claiming that the Maker does not understand what he has made.
Did you know? The chapter describes a surprising reversal of things: Lebanon will become a fruitful field, and the fruitful field will be regarded as a forest—a picture of profound change in reality.
Did you know? In the chapter’s future vision, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of gloom and darkness.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the house of Jacob is described as no longer being ashamed; its descendants will honor the name of the LORD, and those who go astray in spirit and those who complain will gain understanding and accept instruction.
